INDIGNATION MEETING.
Action of the Citizens of the Southern Part of the County in the Rape Case.
Action of the Citizens of the Southern Part of the County in the Rape Case.

A meeting of the citizens of South Giles county was held in the school house near Thompson's mill on Friday, 15th inst.

On motion of Dr. M. S. Waters, J. C. Potts was called to the chair and J. P. Jones made secretary.

By request of the chair, Dr. M. S. Waters stated the object of the meeting to be a general consultation of the people, whereby steps might be taken, in order that justice might be promptly satisfied in the case of Dan Smith, colored, who committed an outrage on the person of Mattie Hendricks a few days since.

After considerable discussion, which was participated in by a number of those present, it was decided to send a memorial to Sheriff Arrowsmith.

On motion of M. W. Roberts, M. S. Waters, I. W. Anderson, Mack Currey, J. M. Howard, J. P. Jones and O. C. Jones were appointed a committee to draft said petition.

The committee reported the following:

NEAR THOMPSON'S MILL,
SOUTH GILES COUNTY,
Oct. 15, 1880.

To H. ARROWSMITH, SH'FF.

We, the citizens of South Giles county, have met to day in council, and have arrived at this conclusion:

That your course in the defense of one Dan Smith, colored, has been of such an extreme as knows no parallel, and is unwarranted by law, in our deliberate and candid judgment.

Now, we must, and do insist, that said Dan Smith, colored, shall be returned to Pulaski for trial, (as promised by yourself), that justice may be met, and that speedily.

We further agree and pledge our selves that we will not in any way molest, or cause said Dan Smith, colored, to be molested, until the court shall have assembled which shallin vestigate his cause.

We further feel that the dignity of law, the character of state, and the safety of our wives and daughters demand this, and should you find it in your heart to ignore these appeals, we denounce you as unworthy of our confidence.

Written in coolness, but never the less in sternness.

As to your action in this matter we request that you give the committee bearing this petition a written answer immediately.

With kind regards, we have the honor to be

YOUR OBEDIENT SERVANTS.

This petition was signed by all the meeting and a number of other substantial citizens, representing the bone and sinew of our land.

On motion it was ordered that a committee of twenty-five should be appointed to wait on Sheriff Arrowsmith and present this petition and receive his reply.

By request of the chair, Dr. Waters appointed the following named gentlemen as said committee: J. P. Jones, W. J. Blassingim, A. J. White, J. M. Howard, F. T. Petty, S. W. Gladish, J. S. Brownlow, J. A. L. Jones, O. C. Jones, C. E. Barnett, R. J. Barnett, A. C. Thompson, R. A. Sherrell, Sidney Locke, M. W. Roberts, Billie Davis, W. J. Hammonds, J. M. McConico, Mack Currey, J. C. Potts, Thos. Nance, W. S. Hopkins, H. T. Mitchell, J. S. Grant and W. C. McRee.

On motion the meeting adjourned until 3 o'clock next day, at which time the committee was ordered to report.

The committee met in Pulaski on Saturday morning, 16th inst., about 9 o'clock. Maj. Stacy kindly tendered the Chancery court room, in which to transact its business. The roll was called, and the committee all present except O. C. Jones and Billie Davis. The latter was represented by proxy, John Case. Dr. Waters being present, was chosen to fill the vacancy occasioned by the absence of Mr. Jones.

Mr. Arrowsmith appeared before the committee, and, after hearing the petition read, asked for a little time to consult before replying, which was granted.

The following was Sheriff Arrowsmith's answer:

In response to your communication, I say that I will use every effort in my power to bring Dan Smith to the speediest trial that can be had under the law, either at a special term, or at the next term in November, now four weeks off, and I will bring him promptly to the jail in Giles county, on the assurances in your petition, and I further request that you appoint one or more of your committee to go with me to Nashville to bring him back. Respectfully,

Oct.16. H. Arrowsmith, Sheriff.

The committee appointed W. J. Blassingim to go with the sheriff to Nashville, and returned and found quite a concourse of people awaiting the sheriff's answer. When it was read they quietly dispersed, seeming to be satisfied.

In justice to Mr. O. C. Jones we state that his absence from the committee was not on account of any disposition on his part to shirk a public duty, but was owing to the sickness of a very valuable horse, which demanded his personal attention. J. C. Ports, Ch'm.

J. P. Jones, Sec'y.

THE NEGRO RAVISHER.
Some Unexpected and Perplexing Difficulties Cropping Out in His Case.
The only event of considerable interest that is likely to transpire in Circuit Court now sitting is the bringing in of the indictment against and the arraignment of Dan Smith, the Shoal creek fiend. Smith is still in the Nashville jail, where he was taken by the sheriff to prevent the insenced people of the vicinity in which he attempted his helmish deed from visiting their wrath upon him summarily. Judge McLemore, as appears from his charge to the grand jury, upholds Sheriff Arrowsmith in his action of removing Smith to Nashville. The question of absorbing interest now is, will Smith be brought here at this term for trial? It cannot be answered yet. It is reported that the witnesses against him will not appear at this term; because they think if they do not appear and no indictment is found, he will be brought to Pulaski and released and will then be out of the sheriff's hands and can be dealt with as he deserves. We do not believe this report. If the witnesses do not apear and no indictment is found, he will be released in Nashville, if at all, and then he will be out of reach. He will not be brought here, as we understand, until the indictment is lodged, and until the witnesses apear the grand jury can find no bill, of course. It depends, therefore, upon the promptness of the witnesses to appear before the grand jury as to whether or not he will be brought here. We urge them to come. The complaint has been that the courts are too tardy in such matters, but if action like this is taken by the witnesses the blame cannot be laid there. Smith ought to be tried speedily and punished severely. Sheriff Arrowsmith did what he conceived to be his duty in running him off, and now he proposes to do as he is directed by the court. Judge McLemore approves his action, but will, unless prevented, see that the law is administered swiftly and surely.

It is useless to conceal the fact that grave apprehensions are entered here that Smith will be taken upon his arrival and hanged by the infuriated people of the country in which the crime was committed. We counsel against this, not on his account, for he more than deserves it; but the court is sitting with every appliance ready for his speedy punishment, and if the law proposes to throw off its tardiness for once and act swiftly, the people should lend it their aid. It is use less to mince words here, however. The people demand Smith's trial and punishment. If they are delayed for any reason, the consequences may be terrible. If they are hastened, we believe the people will allow the law to take its course. Following is the charge of Judge McLemore to the grand jury last Monday upon this point:

I deem it my duty to make a few remarks to the public. I have heretofore had occasion to publicly remark that you had had, since my acquaintance with the county, good sheriffs, and good jurors, and consequently that all guilty men had been punished according to law. But since the last term of my court here, I am informed that the sheriff of your county has had to rescue a prisoner from the hands of a mob determined to hang him, and to send him to another county for safe-keeeping.

What I wish to say is, that mob-law is a remedy for nothing and an aggregation of all evils. In a civilized, law abiding community, like yours has always been, it is an abomination on the face of the earth. There are only three lawful modes of taking human life. One is, in self-defense, when your own life is in imminent peril. Another is, to prevent an atrocious crime, such as rape or murder, when a party is in the act of perpetrating such crime. The other is, when the executioner hangs a man for crime, after indictment, lawful trial and sentence by a competent court.

Now, I am informed that many of the men engaged in this affair are good men and ordinarily law-abiding men, and that they severely censure the sheriff for his action in the premises. Instead of blaming the sheriff you ought to thank him. If the man had been hung, every man engaged in the hanging would have been, in contemplation of law, committing murder. One crime, however dark, does not justify another crime. When the sober, second thought shall return, every upright, honest man engaged in that affair will be thankful that the coolness of the sheriff prevailed over the heated excitement of the crowd. The sheriff simply did his duty and ought to be commended for it by all good men everywhere. The courts are open and Giles county juries have never yet failed to do their duty.

THIRD EDITION
BAD NEGRO HANGED.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., Dec. 2.—Dan'l Smith, colored, who attempted to ravish a young white girl in Giles county some time ago, was sentenced to twenty one years in the penitentiary at Pulaski to day, for assault with intent to commit murder. As soon as this verdict was found a mob rushed into the court room, overpowered the sheriff and posse, seized Smith and dragged him to the street. Four hundred people joined the mob, which took him to a bridge and hanged him until he was dead. The mob came from the vicinity where the crime was committed by Smith.

PULASKI.
Dan Smith, the Kavisher, Hanged By a Mob.
Regular Corr. of the Banner.1
PULASKI. TENN. December
PULASK, TENN., December 2. — Smith, the ravisher, arrived to-day from Nashville on the south-bound train, at two o'clock. A jury was empanelled and the submitted his case, and the extreme penalty of the law in this case was given him—twentv-one years in the state prison. There was quite a crowd in town, and as soon as it was known that he was here, four taps on the court house bell called the crowd together, and they went in the court room and took the prisoner therefrom and proceeded to the bridge across Richmond creek, in the south end of town, and hung him to one of the roof trestles until he was dead. I did not witness the affair, but from what I can gather it was orderly conducted. No one was masked, and the crowd was composed of many of the best men in the county. Everybody to-day says amen to the execution, as Smith's crime was one of the most brutal ever committed in this country. He caught the poor girl by the hair of the head and dragged her two or three hundred yards, even dragging her through a creek. He choked and beat her in a most unmerciful manner, leaving her for dead. He, however, did not accomplish his hellish intentions. We of Giles county are a law-abiding people, but all such deeds as that of Dan Smith will certainly meet with death, be the perpetrator black or white. The unfortunate girl has about recovered from her injuries.

Mr. Porter, upon arriving in Nashville, demanded the negro of the jailer of Davidson county but the latter refused to deliver him up without a special order from Gov. Marks. This was speedily obtained and Mr. Porter, with his prisoner, boarded the morning train for Pulaski, arriving here at about 1:30 o'clock, the train being over an hour late. He brought the negro handcuffed in a roundabout way to the court-house where the judge and a jury were awaiting him. The grand jury immediately brought in its indictment, consisting of two counts—one for assault with attempt to commit rape and the other for assault with attempt to commit murder. Mr. Noble Smithson was appointed counsel for the defendant and the trial proceeded. Meanwhile, suspicions had been aroused and a crowd gathered in the courtroom, but no demonstration was made. The negro, through his counsel, pleaded guilty to both counts of the indictment; the Judge delivered his charge, construing neither offense as punishable with death and the jury promptly returned a verdict of guilty. Sentence was then fixed at 21 years in the penitentiary—the extreme penalty of law. Immediately there was a significant foward movement on the part of the crowd. A rush was made for the prisoner, and the few officers present being unable to protect him he was snatched from their custody and hurried down stairs, somebody in the meantime ringing the court-house bell.

The sound of the bell and the rush and yelling of the crowd from the court-house door were the first intimations that a great many people had of the real state of affairs. In a moment the whole town was in commotion and people came rushing by the scores and hundreds toward the east gate. The negro was borne along by several strong and determined men. Swift, and without noise, they swept down 1st street south, filing west on Flower street to the Presbyterian church, where they halted and it was thought for awhile that they would swing him from the projecting limb of a locust in front of that sacred edifice, but wiser counsels prevailed and a voice was heard to exclaim:

"ON TO THE BRIDGE!"

The march was then resumed. Just before reaching this point the walls of a woman were heard and many heads turned to see a negress wringing her hands and crying piteously: "O, they are going to kill my poor husband! Please let me tell him good bye!" Her prayer was unheeded. She was waved back by the men and soon left in the rear. All this time Dan Smith moved fast or slow at the slightest wish of his captors. Never a word he said—not a murmur or protest—but apparently with willingness kept pace with the crowd. A strong, long sea grass rope was about his neck, with the other end held by determined men, but he needed no pulling, or pushing or urging. Doubtless his senses forsook him when he became fully conscious of the doom that awaited him. The march was kept up until the bridge over Rich land was reached, and then a rush was made to attain eligible positions to witness the consummation of the tragedy. Men clambered up the walls and hung by the rafters and jammed the floor.

About the middle of the bridge they halted and Smith was told to get into a two-horse wagon, there standing. He climbed in hurriedly and stood motionless and expressionless while the noose was carefully adjusted about his neck and the other end thrown over a joist and tied tightly by a man who had climbed there for that purpose.

Here the crowd was called to order and all remained silent to hear the last words of a fiend about to seek companionship with kindred spirits in the dark realms of perdition. A man mounted into the wagon and, addressing the negro, asked him if he had anything to say before he died, but not a word or sign did he make. He stood motionless, the picture of blank despair. Elder William Smith, the gentleman who had mounted into the wagon, proceeded to say that he had raised Dan and partly raised the poor child that he had so brutally outraged; he had read the bible to him and tried in every way to bring him within it blessed influences, but it seemed he had not succeeded, for he now stood there guilty of the most revolting offense in the catalogue of crime, and the people had come to visit their wrath upon him. The speaker was interrupted and forced to desist by the shouts of the multitude:

“DRIVE OUT THE WAGON!”

At length, when the negro had been given time to pray or speak, without making any response, he obeyed an order to mount upon the side of the wagon bed, the vehicle was driven out from under him and he was left dangling in the air. The fall was not sufficient to break his neck and he died from strangulation. He must have suffered intensely, but save a few nervous twitchings and an occasional drawing up of the shoulders, he gave no outward signs of agony. When the rope was taut, the wagon gone and daylight shone between his feet and the floor, a colored woman at the entrance to the bridge, gave vent to a succession of piercing shrieks, while up the street about a hundred yards, alone, and avoided by a crowd of colored women who looked upon her with a dazed expression of countenance that spoke a horrible aversion, stood the woman who called him husband, moaning in unutterable lamentations. When the deed was done the crowd immediately began to disperse, some remaining, to see the tragedy to the end. After he had remained suspended about two hours, Esq. W. F. Alexander, acting coroner, appeared and with assistance cut the body down and placed it in a coffin, holding an inquest and giving a verdict of death by the people. Effort was made to induce some of the colored people in the vicinity to shelter the body for the night, but none of them would allow it to enter their houses, and it was therefore taken to the colored cemetery and left unburied until this morning.

Dan was short but rather heavily built and had a smooth, boyish face which gave no evidence of his beastly propensities. His age appeared to be about 22 and his color approached that of a mulatto. During the march to the bridge he remarked to one of his guards that he was guilty and wanted to die and that whisky was the cause of, his trouble.
Thus Dan Smith met his death.

The court did all it could possibly do to enforce the law.—The fault was in the law itself.—The grand jury, under the proof and the law, could not find a severer indictment than for an attempt to commit rape and murder. The court tried him upon this and under a submission, the jury fixed his term in the penitentiary at 21 years—the utmost limit of the law. Could they do more? The unwritten law that draws a sterner and sharper line of protection before men's family altars has been resorted to; an outraged people have satiated their righteous vengeance; the criminal has expiated his crime with his life. Now let criminations be buried. A terrible example has been made, yet despite the lawlessness of the method, it will have a tendency to throw protection around innocence and virtue. Lynch law is not right, but it must be admitted that Dan Smith suffered justly, for the law was powerless to administer adequate punishment in his case. On the other hands the safety of society depends upon upholding the majesty of the law, and if the latter happens to be defective in a special case, it should be borne in mind that those sworn to administer it as it is, have no right to act upon the presumption of what it should be. An attempt at rape is not a capital offense under the law as it now stands. If the people think it should be, their duty is to instruct their legislators accordingly.
dan-smith-pulaski-1880-12-02.A29:
A NECKSECUTION.
The Appropriate Ending of a Lecherous Villain.
PULASKI, Dec. 2. — Dan Smith, the negro who ravished a little white girl, Mattie Hendricks, on Oct 11, in the second district of Giles county, was taken from the court-house here to-day and lynched. He had been previously removed to Nashville to protect him against violence. He was brought down on the 1:30 train and carried to the courthouse, where he was immediately tried. He plead guilty to the charge and was sentenced to twenty-one years' imprisonment in the penitentiary—the extreme penalty of the law. Smith was heard to complain at the severity of the punishment.

The sheriff intended to return with him to Nashville on the 2:15 train. News of the trial becoming noised abroad, a mob of 800 to 1,000 men quickly collected, and although the sheriff and his posse offered a determined resistance, they were overpowered and the mob took the prisoner away determined to administer justice at their own hands. They carried him down Main street to the bridge that spans the romantic Richland creek. A rope, one end of which was tied around Smith's neck, was fastened to a beam of the bridge. Rev. Wm. Smith, the man who raised Dan, got into the wagon and prayed for him. The preacher also raised the victim of the negro's devilish design. While Mr. Smith was talking one man cried out, "This man dies for the safety of the whole people." The affair was a terrible one, but no more so than the fiendish deed for which he was executed. The affair occupied a very few minutes.
dan-smith-pulaski-1880-12-02.A30: On last Thursday a colored man named Dan Smith was hung by a mob at Pulaski, Tenn. The charge against Smith was, of course, attempted outrage upon a white girl. He had been tried in Court, and sentenced to 21 years in the Penitentiary, but the chivalry thought the punishment too light. This charge of "attempted rape" seems to be a very common one in the South, and the charge is generally considered, down there, sufficient ground for murder. As it is always a colored man charged with attacking a white woman, it seems strange—the dangerous character of the colored men being known—that the white women will persist in wandering about in convenient localities for the terrible "niggers" to catch them in. At least, it seems so to a calm observer away up North.

election-riot-johnston-1880-11-02.A13:
HOW IS THIS ?
We quote the following dispatches from the Oregonian:

CHICAGO, Nov. 4.—The probable Republican victory in North Carolina is believed here to be quite positive. The Republicans of that State may cause surprise by their work.

EDGEFIELD, Nov. 4.—One negro killed and eleven wounded in an election riot.

MEMPHIS, Tenn.; Nov. 4.—The Republicans gain two Congressmen in Tennessee and elect the Governor. Moon is probably elected here to Congress by 1,000 majority. The Republicans gain 11 assemblymen and claim the legislature by virtue of other gains in middle and east Tennessee.

How is it possible that this condition of affairs could be true when the Oregonian has been insisting that no Republican could vote in the South?

Surely the Oregonian has been editorially lying all through the campaign or its dispatches lie.

The fact is, neither North Carolina or Tennessee have gone Republican, nor have the Republicans carried a single State in the South. But it does seem curious to every consistent reader of a newspaper that it should charge one way for six months and then claim the contrary the day after election.

O, Consistency, thou art a jewel—and thy name is Oregonian!

The Election.
Since our last publication the world has been informed of the election of James A. Garfield, of Ohio, the Republican candidate, to the highest office in the world—that of President of the United States. The Democratic party has been incontestably beaten, and it becomes us as good citizens to abide the result without a murmur. Whatever doubts the world may have had of the election of President Hayes it can have no misgivings as to the election of Garfield. It requires more manhood to sustain ourselves under defeat than in success, and we hope that our people will be now, as they ever have been in the past, equal to the occasion. We should give way to no unmanly murmurings, but should accept the situation in good faith, and yield gracefully to the will of the majority. Democratic principles make the demand that we should accept Garfield as our President as gracefully as we should have expected the Republicans to accept Hancock as their President, had he been elected.

In the election of Garfield we see nothing to prevent our continued prosperity as a nation or as individuals. The financial policy of the country, we presume, will not be disturbed and it is certain that the husbandman will be rewarded for his labor in the future as fully as he has been paid in the past. The Constitution of the United States protects us from aggression by the party in power at Washington, and a wise Democratic State Government in Columbia will insure peace and prosperity to our people, if they will only devote their undivided energies as becomes good and peaceable citizens, to the work of building up their own individual fortunes. Garfield's name has been smirched by charges of corruption, but it must be acknowledged that he is a man of ability. Having been born in a cabin, without friends, and having made his way by regular and constant steps until he has reached the highest office within the gift of the people, it is not to be wondered at that he should have made some missteps on the way. The man who could rise to that exalted position without doing some act to which his opponents could object, would be a prodigy indeed. We take it that Garfield is about as good as the average politician, and that a man of his ability and success in life is not born to hate. Men who have the faculty to hate, well developed, seldom rise to high position; and while political aspirants are governed by extreme men, it is a well-known fact, when a man takes the oath and assumes the duties of office, that he is governed entirely by the conservative sentiment. With these facts before us we think we have reason to hope that Garfield will make a good President for the whole country. While it is to be regretted that we have been so signally defeated in the contest for National honors, yet we have the glorious reflection that, with the exception of Beaufort, Orangeburg, and Sumter, South Carolina is Democratic from the mountains to the sea. With good county and State Governments we shall not be cast down for the reverse which we have experienced in the Presidential contest. Taking it, all in all, we have cause to be thankful that we are in as good a condition as we are.

Lec vs. Richardson.
Representative John S. Richardson, of South Carolina, having been permitted to occupy Mr. J. H. Rainey's seat in Congress for the past two years, has recently subscribed to some very silly allegations in reply to Judge Lee's notice of contest for a seat in the Forty-seventh Congress. Mr. Richardson fails to answer a single one of the startling accusations contained in Judge Lee's notice, but alleges that the latter is not a citizen of South Carolina, and therefore was ineligible to a seat in Congress.

The facts on that point are these: Judge Lee is a native of Sumter, South Carolina, where he resided uninterruptedly—except while in college—until 1878, when the lawless Democracy of Sumter County, of which Mr. Richardson is the recognized leader, drove him out of the State, forcing him to vacate the judge of probate's office. During the early months of 1879 he resided in this city until he received assurances of protection from outrage, when he returned to his home. The following year he was sent as a delegate to the Chicago convention. Subsequently he was unanimously nominated for Congress. Mr. Richardson must be driven to a pitiable strait when he is forced to adopt the silly pretext that his antagonist is not a citizen of the State, and therefore ineligible.

Judge Lee's citizenship is quite as well established as is that of Mr. Richardson. When the Forty-seventh Congress assembles we think Mr. Richardson will discover that he has been reckoning without his host when he concluded that a Republican House would permit him to retain a seat secured by the most glaring of frauds, simply because his contestant had to flee from his State to avoid the prosecution of Democratic thugs.

MURDER IN NEW MEXICO.
Colonel Charles Potter, of the U. S. Geological Survey, Murdered-- The Three Murderers Swung Up By Vig- ilanton.
Special to the Herald.

Alburquerque, N. M., Jan. 31. — Colonel Charles Potter, of the United States geological survey, who had for some time been collecting statistics for the census bureau, left Alburquerque October 14th, 1880, for the New Placer mining camp. He was seen the next day at Tjera, N. M., traveling toward San Antonita. Since then nothing has been heard of him and his fate had been shrouded in mytery, until a few days ago when Sheriff Armijo, of Bernallillo county, obtained some evidence implicating one Escallero Parera. Measures were at once taken and he was arrested at Isletta, N. M., and brought to this city. He at first denied all knowledge of the affair, but at length confessed that he had been a witness of the crime, though not a sharer in it. He said that Colonel Potter had been waylaid in a lonely canon near San Antonita, and after a desperate resistance had been killed. His body was then robbed and buried. Sheriff Armijo at once started for the spot, accompanied by Perara. He returned to night, bringing Colonel Potter's body, which was found near Ojo Chilal, three miles from Tijero. He also captured two other men, Liguel Barrera and a Mexican known as "California Joe." Another Mexican, who had a share in the murder, named Pantaleon Liera, was hanged by vigilantes at Bernalillo a few weeks ago for horse-stealing, and if public sentiment goes for anything Perre, Barrara and California Joe will follow in his footsteps before another day.

FRONTIER FIENDS.
Col. Potter's Fate.
Fn. New Mexico
SANDA FE, New Mexico.—Sheriff Armujo, of Bernalillo county, upon the receipt of the News that a man named Escalastico Piere had been implicated in the murder of Col. Potter, who was in the employ of the interior department to collect mining statistics for the cusus bureau, sent two men with a warrant for his arrest. He was found at Isleta, fifteen miles below Alburque. The man denied any knowledge until confronted by the sheriff, when he stated stated the following facts, which he said had been related to him by one of the parties to the murder, named Marino Leybor, the leader of the gang. He was placed in jail and securely guarded, as the mob was determined to lynch him. The following day the sheriff with six well-armed men, and accompanied by Mr. F. O. Van Zandt Col. Potter's intimate and faithful friend started for the place where the body of Col. Potter was left. About twenty-five miles from Alburque they left the road and following a trail came upon the dead bodies of two horses, one Col. Potter's and the other one of the robbers. A pile of ashes and half-burnt brush was designated by Escalastico as containing the remains of the murdered man. A search being instituted, a few boxes, some scraps of clothing, and a number of peculiar buttons were found. The later were identified by Mr. Van Zandt as belonging to Col. Potter. Escalastico, who had strenuously denied having been a witness to the murder, influenced by natural fear through the menaces of his captors, then gave, as all have reason to believe, a truthful account of the tragedy. The colonel who left Tejaharas that morning Oct. 5, met two men upon the road, from whom he inquired the direction to Las Placas. They directed him to a trail purposely to mislead him, he being at the time on the direct road. When they separated, the two men made a deter, and reaching a point which Potter was to pass, saw him dismount and in the act of lighting his pipe. Then they opened fire on him, the first shot striking on the knee and causing him to fall to the ground. Potter drew his weapon and shot one of his assailants in the arm. The second shot took effect in Potter's breast, and his return fire killed a horse of one of the robbers. Potter's horse then fell dead and in a few seconds later was followed by the unfortunate master. The bandits after ridding the body of all but the clothes they doing too bloody to safely take, covered it with brush, which being fired, soon as they thought, destroyed all traces of their crime. Further inquiry elicited the fact that two of the assailants of Potter were living in the mountains not far from the spot of the murder, and a party at once surrounded their house effecting their capture. The same means that had been so successfully employed in the instance of Escalante produced a confirmatory confession from them, with the additional information that the robber who had been wounded by Potter was no less personage than Marino Leybor. He had been known to have presented a watch to Pintleton Mira, being about a month ago at Bernallilo on charge of murder and theft. This watch answered the description of the one worn by Col. Potter and, the fact of Marino appearing the same time with a wounded arm, which injury he ascribed to a fall from his horse, convicts him in the minds of all men as one of Potter's murders. The watch was traced from the hands of Mira to a pawn-broker in Albuquerque, but the case had already been melted when a demand for it was made by the sheriff. Sheriff Armajo, who has been indefatigable in his endeavors to capture the gang now, since through the confession of parties in his hands he has the names and rendezvous of the remainder of
the horde, trusts to be able to bring
them all to justice, and thus rid this
country of as desperate a set of men as
it has been the fate of any country to
cursed with.

Hanged to a Tree.
Columbus, O., Sept. 1.—Thos. McDonald, aged 28 years, a farmer living near Commercial Point, Pickaway county, was taken from his house last night by men and hanged to a tree near his residence. tom-mcdaniel-commercial-point-1880-11.A10:
THE HISTORY OF A NOTORIOUS ROUGH,

And the Sudden Stop Put to His Career of Crime—The Lynching of a Man Who Has Terrorized Pickaway County, O., For the Past Ten Years.

Columbus, O., September 2.—The following additional details of the hanging of Thomas McDaniels, at Commercial Point, Pickaway County, and the causes which led to the act, have been received here from that place:

For the past ten years McDaniels has terrorized the section of country in which he lived, engaging in all sorts of devilish and diabolical tricks with impunity. His chief passion has been to cut, carve and shoot; his greatest weakness has been for

Brass-Handled Pistols and Two-Edged Knives.

He came to this country when a lad fourteen years old. His home was formerly at Falmouth, Kentucky, from whence he fled to escape arrest for engaging in a cutting scrape. He knocked around at odd jobs, and about ten years ago he began work for Mr. Decker, a large land owner, as a farm hand. He was a fellow of fine address, and at that time was a handsome man. Mr. Decker's, Glice, and ran off with her when she was only sixteen, and was married to her. The elopement created great scandal and excitement in the neighborhood and the girl's brothers, Boone and Peter Decker, swore they would kill Tom on sight.

Notwithstanding their threats Tom returned in a week from his bridal trip, rode into the Point with his brass pistols and his bride,

Panting for Goro and Eager for a Fray that would enable them to decimate the Decker heirs, and thus increase his wife's share of her father's vast property.

Shortly after his marriage he attended a wolf hunt at Bloomfield, and on his way through the Point he became offended at Thomas Becket, a dry goods merchant, and getting off his horse, he proceeded to hammer Mr. Becket, a hundred persons standing by afraid to interfere.

A bystander finally pulled him off and prevented him braining Becket with a piece of buggy shaft.

Several years ago there was housewarming near Barron's Cavern in the southern part of Franklin, and Tom

Went Down Without An Invitation to help warm the house and the guests. In the midst of the dance he provoked a quarrel by stepping on the toe of a country gentleman who was fastidious enough to object, and whipping out one of his brass pistols, he began firing into the crowd and brought down a man named Hock Breckenridge by shooting him in the thigh. Tom was not arrested for this eccentric contribution to the evening's entertainment.

Later he turned detective, and went to arrest a man named Crawford near Mt. Sterling who was charged with throwing stones at a train on the Muskingum Valley near Washington C. H. He rushed into the room where Crawford was eating a meal,

Shot Him in the Face, and then arrested him. He was never molested for this little pleasantry by the officers of the law.

About a year ago he became enamored of a fair maiden of doubtful repute at the American House, in Darbyville. He never stopped to inquire whether his intentions would be agreeable, but called on her one night when the village was wrapped in slumber, by climbing on a peddler's wagon and going through the window. On the inside he found a gentleman, called a sport, named O. S. Renick, who gave Tom a warm welcome. They fought over the room and stairs until the

House Was as Bloody as a Butcher's Pen.

His last escapades are numerous and of recent date. A short time since he was taken to Circleville and put in jail for stealing a buggy. He went to a neighbor's house, hitched his horse to a new buggy and drove off. Wood Hoffman interested himself and secured Tom's release by putting up money on a guarantee that he (Tom) had plenty of money at home, and would refund at once. Wood went home with him, and found that neither Tom nor his wife had a dollar in the house; so he took Tom's buggy. Tom then went to Jacktown and cut up the new buggy he had once stolen.

Tom's latest ambition has been to

Thrash the Entire Population of Commercial Point, and he has threatened after doing this to lay the place in ashes.

This spring he was out squirrel hunting with an old-fashioned shot gun. In firing it a piece of the cap flew into his right eye, which ran out of the socket. He paid no attention to it, and went about as if nothing had happened. He didn't seem to know what pain was.

Abut a month ago he went into Martin Beaver's place, at the Point. Martin runs a grocery and a threshing machine. and is one of the local magnates. He is a magnificent specimen of physical manhood and a relative of Tom's wife. He had taken a dislike to Mart. because he would not let him turn everything topsy turvy when he got filled up with liquor. About a month since Tom entered

Meant to Shoot Him Down.

Mart did not wait for him to execute his threat but grappled him, and they fought all over the house, McDaniel getting the worst of it, and Beaver took his pistols from him.

Last Monday Tom played his last act. He entered Beaver's place with a knife in his hand, and announced that he had come to wind up Beaver's mortal career. Beaver grappled him before he could execute his threat, knocked the knife out of his hand, and then they had it rough and tumble pounding and pummeling. Beaver tried to gouge Tom's good eye out, and thus terminate his powers for mischief. A bystander says he had it out two or three times, and tried to pull it out and it would snap back with a report like

A Cork Flying Out of a Champagne Bottle and all this time Tom never winced. One man says: "I have been in the army and all over the South, and seen all sorts of characters, but Tom McDaniel was the most desperate and gamest man I ever saw."

McDaniel was taken home to the care of his distracted wife, whose devotion never faltered, and under her care, with medical aid, Tom was slowly recovering the use of his only eye.

Last night, about half-past 11, his wife got up to bathe a cloth and lay it on his eye. She had just done this and was closing the door, which had stood open during the hot evening, when about eight armed men appeared and ordered her to leave the room. She complied without asking a word or screaming.

She Knew the End Had Come. There was no attempt at disguise. As the wife went out Tom was surrounded in bed, and as he straightened up he said:

"Boys, are you going to kill me?"
There was no reply. His hands were bound and a noose, made out of a halter-rope, was slipped over his head and tightened about his neck. He was led out. No, he was dragged out. Eight stout men laid hold of the rope. Not a word was spoken.

The programme had been arranged, the tree selected, and the leader, with a cocked revolver, bossed the job in silence. They dragged him over a rail fence, over logs and through bushes for about four hundred yards to a little red oak near the road side.

Where He Was Strung Up.
He never spoke after he left the house. This morning the early passers by were horror-struck to see a nude body swinging to a limb. It was after 8 o'clock before the Justice of the Peace, 'Squire Beaver, arrived and ordered the body taken down. It was nude, except the band of the shirt around the neck and a strip down the back, on which was written the following card in a wretched scrawl:

"Take Notice!
"Any or all persons interfering will meet the same fate. We will protect all law-abiding citizens.

"VIGILANCE COMMITTEE."

'Squire Beaver held an inquest, examining the wife and five other witnesses. The testimony covers the facts given above. The coroner's verdict was a "death by person or persons unknown."

The hanging was well done. There was no mob. There were not over twenty persons in the party, probably not over ten. Part of them came up the road from Jacktown, and the remainder down from the Point. They met at the gate on the Decker farm, under the shadow of the tree where he was hanged. The limb on which he was hanged was Picked Out by a Committee Some Weeks Ago.

The Vigilantes have made two efforts to hang him before, but when they called at the house he was never at home, and they disguised their mission so as not to arouse suspicion.

The body, when cut down, presented a frightful appearance. The chest was literally skinned. The left nipple had been torn off the breast, and the scars, scratches and bruises indicate the horrible and brutal treatment he had received before being hanged. He was buried at 5 o'clock, people flocking to the funeral from miles around.

This is the first hanging and lynching that ever occurred in Pickaway since it has been a county.

The Slaughter of Tom McDonald.
The tribulations of Tom McDonald, of Pick
The tribulations of Tom McDonald, of Pickaway County, Ohio, and the terrorism for years sown by his presence in the vicinity of Commercial Point, has suddenly, and if all reports are true, brutally terminated. Some time ago M. V. Beavers, of Commercial Point, had a difficulty with McDonald, and being a very muscular man, is said to have given him a terrible whipping. McDonald, a noted desperado, and a curse to those about him, was much humiliated by this unexpected turn in his personal encounters, and a few days ago, under the influence of liquor, he visited Beavers, who keeps a store, with a view to settling the matter. He had no sooner displayed a knife and stated his object than Beavers promptly knocked him known and gave him a terrible beating, kicking him about the head and face until he become unrecognizable. The only eye the desperado had was forced from its socket out upon his check. Beavers left him lying in the gutter, where he remained several hours, no one seeming to care to volunteer to remove him. Finally he was taken to his home on a dray, almost in a dying condition, where he was cared for by his family, consisting of his wife, two children and a man named Ryan. About midnight the dogs began barking, and Ryan, fearing a mob, told McDonald's wife of his surmises. She went to the door to get Tom a drink, and when she opened it, in stalked twelve men, all of them disguised, with visors over their faces, and each carrying a revolver ready for instant action. Quickly divining their purpose, Tom cried out in an agony of terror, "For God's sake don't let them in." But the desperate men pressed through the door and into the room, and to the bed where he lay, almost dead from his wounds of the day before. The affrighted woman stood speechless, afraid to speak or offer any resistance. Without a word they jerked him out of bed in his night clothes, when he shrieked aloud, but his mouth was soon closed by strong hands, and he was carried bodily out of the house. Reaching the yard, a rope halter was placed around his neck, and the men taking a hold on that they ran at full speed at least three hundred yards from the house to the place appointed for the execution. Over fences, roads, and through fields they dragged the naked body of poor Tom, never stopping for any obstruction until they reached a small red-oak tree, perhaps fifteen yards from the pile, and there he was strung up. We have a somewhat comical illustration of the rigid idolity with which the Prussian soldier is wont to carry out instructions imparted by those set in authority over him in an incident that took place the other evening during a performance of "Fidelio" at the Town Theatre of Mayence. Herr Stain, the leading baritone of the company, was about, in the character of the wicked Don Pizarro, to undergo the penalty of his evil deeds, the stage "business" requiring that he should be led away to confinement by two guards at a sign from the Minister of State. The brace of "supers" told off for this duty were private soldiers belonging to an artillery regiment in garrison at Mayence—two sturdy Brandonbergers, drilled and disciplined to a niece. As they took up the position assigned to them on either side of Pizarro, previous to marching him on the stage, the chorist intrusted with the port of "officer commanding escort" whispered to them, "Remember, the man is a State prisoner; guard him carefully." Obedient to orders, they led Pizarro away to his dressing-room, where he rapidly exchanged his theatrical costume for private clothes, and, opening his door, was about to go home to supper as usual, when, to his amazement, he found his passage barred by a couple of crossed halberds. A MYSTERY.

DENVEN, Colo., Nov. 28.—There seems to be some mystery about the shooting of Lt-Gov. Robinson, at Robinson Camp, last night. The particulars so far heard are these: There was a dispute about the possession of a mine there, and a guard had been placed to watch it. Last night Gov. Robinson and the manager of the mine went to it after dark. The guard, not recognizing them, and not having an answer to the inquiry as to who they were, fired, he says, into the rock overhead. Gov. Robinson fell, shot in four places. He is still living, but his wounds are believed to be fatal. The fact that there had been trouble between the miners and manager during the last week, the guard's story and the peculiarity of the wounds make the theory that it was accidental unsatisfactory.

SHARPE DEALINGS.

DAYTON, O., Nov. 23.—Last night the firm of Augustus Sharpe & Co., one of the largest dry-goods houses in Dayton, was closed by the Sheriff, and warrants issued for the arrest of Sharpe, charging him with obtaining goods of Eastern firms under false pretenses. It is said that he gave a deed for a farm in Indiana to a clerk named Pierce as a basis for him to open business in Lancaster, O., and subsequently attached the goods bought by his clerk, amounting to about $30,000. The attorneys of Sharpe say that the creditors of Pierce are angry because Sharpe got in ahead of them, and want to force him to permit Pierce to make an arrangement.

TRAIN-ROBBERS.

SPECIAL DISPATCH TO THE CHICAGO TRIBUNE.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Nov. 28.—Late Saturday night Dick Talby and Dick Rose, two men living in the eastern part of Jackson County, were arrested at Independence for complicity in the robbery of the Chicago & Alton train at Glendale, in October, 1879. They were indicted by the Grand Jury last week on the evidence of Daniel Bansham, who confessed to being one of the robbers. Both men are confined in the Second Street Jail, but refuse to be interviewed, simply saying that their arrest was a complete surprise to them, but intimate that some startling developments will be made at their trial. Other arrests will soon be made, but who the parties are is not known.

SENTENCED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

JANESVILLE, Wis., Nov. 27.—This morning Henry L. Phillips, late telegraph operator for the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway at Bololt, appeared in the Circuit Court to receive his sentence for the larceny of $180 at one time and $115 at another from the office of the Railroad Company where he was employed. He had pleaded guilty to these two charges. Judge Conger passed sentence, fixing the punishment for the first offense at two years in the State's Prison, and for the second offense two and a half years, to commence at the expiration of the first sentence.

MURDER-TRIAL.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Nov. 28.—The evidence in the Maher and Norris murder-trial has closed, and nearly all of Saturday was occupied in arguing. Prosecutor Collins opened for the State, speaking several hours. He was followed by Col. Dick Do Hart for the defense, who spoke until half-past 3, when Court adjourned over until Monday. Col. Billy Wilson is to speak in behalf of the prisoners, and Capt. Carnnahan will close. The case will hardly reach the jury before Tuesday.

ABOUT A GIRL.

Quincy, Ill., Nov. 27.—Last evening a row occurred at a country dance at Newman's distillery, near Seehom Station, on the south line of Adams County, in which a young man named Brewer, son of a widow living there, was cut on the cheek, on the breast, and on his hand by a man named Seward. The quarrel was over a girl. Brewer, it is said, will die. Seward fled and has not been arrested. Officers are in pursuit.

A NEGRO DESPERADO KILLED.
HUNTSVILLE, Ala., Nov. 27.—A negro by the name of William Towey was killed yesterday near this city by Deputy-Sheriff Cooper and Special Deputy W. J. Franks. The officers had a writ of arrest for Towey, and were endeavoring to serve it, when Towey raised a loaded shotgun and presented it at the officers, who immediately fired and killed him. Towey, it is said, was a desperate character.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Nov. 27.—James Tierney, of East St. Louis, was brought here today by a Deputy Marshal. He is charged with illegal voting in having gone over into Missouri and voted at the recent election. He was transferred to the custody of the Missouri authorities.

Indiana's Electorial Muddle.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.
